prize_parts.citation: For the optical lattice clock: the magic-wavelength trapping scheme and its development into many-atom clocks of 10^-18 accuracy and record stability.

statement.case_for: I keep B031 with Katori and Ye as my single-part position, and the round-1 exchange has not changed the configuration. The discovery is one idea with one consequence: choosing the lattice wavelength so that the light shift of the clock transition cancels removes the conflict between tight confinement and an unperturbed transition, so that very many atoms are interrogated at once in the Lamb-Dicke regime. The measurable result is fractional uncertainty near 10^-18, reproduced by independent laboratories, together with stability that single-ion clocks cannot match because of atom number. That is a finding about how to isolate a quantum system from its environment, and it has already been used for redshift measurements over centimetre height differences and for bounds on drifting constants. The credit is two names, concept and realisation, which I find easier to defend than the trio-from-a-larger-group allocations that the competing candidates require. After the chair's summary I also see that B031 and B016 are the two live leads and that the choice between them turns on lineage versus adjacency, not on any dispute about reality or maturity of either result.
statement.case_against: The lineage objection is real and the exchange has not removed it: the 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize covered control of single trapped ions, and a third award on the same measurement ecosystem will be read by some as a continuation. I now think my round-1 appeal to the pending redefinition of the second was the weakest part of my case, because Johansson and Mehlig are right that the discovery stands on the 10^-18 comparisons and does not need a standards decision to validate it, so I drop it as a reason for urgency. Attribution also remains open at the edges, since Lemonde, Lisdat, Takamoto, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups lie outside the two names, and the citation must be worded around the lattice scheme and many-atom performance to hold. Finally, circuit QED has seven-of-eight breadth in the opening rankings, which I treat as a weak signal but not as nothing.

responses.point: Mehlig argued that the pending redefinition of the second is no reason to act now, because the clock result is secure whether or not the second is redefined, and that the 2005 comb prize partly covers the same metrological ground; he regards the conceptual step as smaller than the engineering.
responses.response: I concede the first point entirely: I should not have presented the redefinition as timeliness, and I have removed it from my case. On the second point I disagree with the weighting. The comb prize gave a way to count optical cycles; it said nothing about how to hold a large ensemble of neutral atoms without the trap perturbing the transition. The magic-wavelength condition is a conceptual step in the same sense that the Paul and Penning traps were: a way to confine without disturbing, with its own physics in polarisabilities, hyperpolarisability and collisional shifts. Calling it engineering undersells why accuracy and stability both moved by orders of magnitude. I accept that this is partly a judgment of taste, as you say, but I would ask you to compare it with circuit QED on the same test, where I also see a clear idea but one whose payoff is architecture for a technology that has not yet delivered its decisive outcome.

responses.point: Johansson regards B031 as the best fallback if circuit QED is judged too close to the 2025 prize, and would not tie a prize to a metrological decision still pending; he also says the 2025 award was for macroscopic tunnelling and that the circuit QED credit boundary around Girvin and Huang is open.
responses.response: I accept your correction on urgency. On the chair's question about the two leads I would answer as follows. I do not think the 2025 prize bars circuit QED on scientific grounds: macroscopic tunnelling and strong single-photon coupling are different physics, and a careful citation can say so. My concern is the credit, since you and Mehlig both accept that Girvin and Huang sit inside the founding proposal and a trio of Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf leaves a theory name out that the 2004 paper itself does not rank below Blais. B031 has no comparable internal boundary: Katori proposed the scheme and Ye drove it to the accuracy and stability frontier. I note, and appreciate, that you flagged your institutional proximity, and I would suggest that if B016 advances the committee weigh your support with that disclosure in mind, as would apply to Lindroth's ETH link. On that basis I regard B016 as my first alternative and not as a lesser candidate.

responses.point: Lindroth would put the early strontium work by several groups and the many-body clock physics in Ye's laboratory into the citation, and says a third seat would be the hardest call and should not be filled without clear evidence of priority.
responses.response: I agree and have changed the citation wording accordingly. The first lattice-clock demonstrations came from more than one group within a short span, and what separates Ye's contribution is the route to 10^-18 and the many-atom stability, so the citation now names the many-atom accuracy and stability and does not claim first demonstration of the clock transition. I also agree with you that a third name should be added only on clear priority evidence. Having reread the shortlist for this, I cannot identify a person for whom that evidence is established on what we have, so I stay at two names and treat Lemonde, Lisdat, Takamoto and Ludlow as part of the discussion record, not as a reason to widen.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B016 as the most broadly ranked candidate with the clearest attribution, treats the 2025 prize as the main exposure, and sees clocks as a close alternative whose citation might read as a continuation of 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: I take your point about breadth seriously, since a candidate ranked by all eight members is a hard fact about the room, but I would not let breadth substitute for the scientific question. On lineage, I would put the test this way: could the citation for B031 be written without naming a comb or a trapped ion? It can, because it names a trapping condition and the performance it enables. The citation for B016 faces the mirror problem that you identify, to distinguish itself from 2025, and I think both candidates can meet their test. What would change my ordering is not a support count but evidence on credit, namely a reading of the 2004 papers showing that Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf carry the founding credit without Girvin and Huang, or evidence that early lattice-clock priority belongs to a group outside Katori and Ye.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers the experimental Higgs discovery with Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee as founders, regards clocks as an invention whose decisive payoff has not arrived, and says the committee should recognise a discovery first.
responses.response: I respect the argument that a new particle is the cleanest kind of discovery, and I do not dispute the physics. My difficulty is the same one your own case_against states, and I think it is decisive for me: the credit is spread across two collaborations of thousands and the three-name set is a compromise between founders and discovery-era leaders that you yourself say Gianotti could displace. I cannot judge the roles of the named individuals from the shortlist, and I would not vote for a configuration whose names I cannot defend. On your point about invention versus discovery, I would say the lattice clock is a discovery of a condition under which a trapped ensemble becomes a clock: the cancellation of the light shift at the magic wavelength was predicted, then found to work, and then used to measure things that were previously out of reach. That is as much about nature as an instrument.

uncertainties: Whether the full committee regards a two-person lattice-clock prize as defensible given the early priority history involving Lemonde, Lisdat, Takamoto, Ludlow and others.
Whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes make a third award on the same measurement lineage unattractive, which I cannot resolve by argument alone.
Whether the credit boundary around Girvin and Huang would, on a closer reading of the 2004 papers, move me towards or away from B016.
I cannot rule out that my own field proximity leads me to overvalue the clock candidate.
statement.conflict_note: No direct conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. A connection to report remains: I spent part of my doctoral period in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall's 2005 prize is part of the lineage on which Ye's work builds, so I may be seen as close to that tradition. I am an atomic physicist at Lund working on laser spectroscopy and laser stabilisation, which overlaps methodologically with this field, though I have no documented collaboration with the candidates. I also note that my Lund collaborations (Rippe, Walther, Kinos), WACQT and Deep Light Vision concern quantum memories and quantum technology, so they bear on B016 and B028 only indirectly; I flag them again in case either becomes central. No new conflict arose from the first-round exchange.
